prompt: Why does Alice find sitting by her sister tiresome?
options: She has nothing to do while sitting there.
Her sister keeps interrupting her reading.
She is worried about getting home before dark.
She has already finished making a daisy-chain.
explanation: The opening describes Alice as tired because she has been sitting with nothing to do; it mentions no quarrel or urgent errand.
sourceQuote: very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do

prompt: What does Alice dislike about the book her sister is reading?
options: It is too difficult for her to understand.
It has no pictures or conversations.
It describes things Alice already knows.
It is too short to hold her attention.
explanation: Alice notes both missing features and wonders what use a book has without them; she does not complain about its print or topic.
sourceQuote: it had no pictures or conversations in it

prompt: How does the hot day affect Alice?
options: It makes her eager to run around.
It makes her sleepy and stupid.
It keeps her from hearing her sister.
It makes the flowers difficult to see.
explanation: The narrator says the hot day makes Alice feel sleepy and stupid, rather than energetic or unable to hear.
sourceQuote: the hot day made her feel very sleepy and stupid

prompt: What is Alice weighing up when she thinks about making a daisy-chain?
options: Whether she likes daisies enough to keep them.
Whether her sister would want a chain too.
Whether she should wait until the day cools.
Whether the pleasure is worth getting up to pick daisies.
explanation: Alice considers whether making the chain is worth getting up and picking daisies, so she weighs the pleasure against the effort.
sourceQuote: making a daisy-chain would be worth the trouble of getting up

prompt: How does the narrator describe Alice's first reaction to the Rabbit speaking?
options: She immediately decides it must be dreaming.
At the time, it seems quite natural to her.
She asks the Rabbit to repeat what it said.
She runs away before noticing the Rabbit.
explanation: Although a talking rabbit should seem strange, the narrator says Alice thought it natural at first and reflected later.
sourceQuote: she ought to have wondered at this, but at the time it all seemed quite natural

prompt: What does seeing the Rabbit use a watch lead Alice to do?
options: Call to her sister for help.
Look for another watch in the grass.
Run after it, curious about its pocket and watch.
Wonder whether its pink eyes are real.
explanation: The watch in a waistcoat pocket is unfamiliar to Alice; curiosity makes her run after the Rabbit.
sourceQuote: a watch to take out of it, and burning with curiosity, she ran across the field after it

prompt: When Alice follows the Rabbit down the hole, what does she not consider?
options: How she will get out again.
Whether Dinah will miss her.
How deep the hole might be.
Whether the Rabbit is hurt.
explanation: The narration says she follows the Rabbit down without once considering how she might return to the surface.
sourceQuote: never once considering how in the world she was to get out again

prompt: How does the rabbit-hole change before Alice begins falling?
options: It turns sharply upward into a tunnel.
It opens onto a garden path.
It narrows until she must crawl.
It runs straight, then dips suddenly down.
explanation: The tunnel first continues straight, then suddenly dips, sending Alice into a deep well rather than back into the field.
sourceQuote: The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel for some way, and then dipped suddenly down

prompt: What explanation does the narrator offer for Alice having time to look around as she falls?
options: She has stopped falling for a moment.
The well may be very deep, or she may fall very slowly.
The Rabbit has slowed the fall from below.
The shelves are close enough to catch her.
explanation: The narrator offers two possible explanations, great depth or a very slow fall, without deciding which is true.
sourceQuote: Either the well was very deep, or she fell very slowly

prompt: What prevents Alice from seeing what lies below her?
options: The well is too narrow.
The Rabbit blocks her view.
It is too dark to see anything.
The cupboards hide the bottom.
explanation: Alice first tries to see what lies below, but the passage says darkness prevents her from seeing anything.
sourceQuote: it was too dark to see anything

prompt: What does Alice notice along the sides of the well?
options: Doors and lamps set into the walls.
Cupboards and bookshelves, with maps and pictures on pegs.
Baskets of food and folded blankets.
Windows looking out over a garden.
explanation: The well's sides contain cupboards and bookshelves, with maps and pictures hanging on pegs; the passage mentions no windows or lamps there.
sourceQuote: they were filled with cupboards and book-shelves; here and there she saw maps and pictures hung upon pegs

prompt: Why does Alice put the jar into a cupboard instead of dropping it?
options: She fears it could hurt somebody underneath.
She wants to hide it from the Rabbit.
She plans to take it into the garden.
She hopes to keep the marmalade fresh.
explanation: She fears the jar could kill somebody underneath, so she carefully puts it into a cupboard instead of dropping it.
sourceQuote: she did not like to drop the jar for fear of killing somebody underneath

prompt: Why does Alice repeat what she learned in school even though nobody is listening?
options: She is trying to remember the Rabbit's name.
She hopes someone below will answer.
She treats saying it aloud as good practice.
She wants to prove she can calculate the distance.
explanation: Alice knows no one is listening, but treats repeating what she learned in lessons as useful practice.
sourceQuote: there was no one to listen to her, still it was good practice to say it over

prompt: What does Alice's use of “Latitude” and “Longitude” reveal?
options: She has studied maps of the well.
She does not know what either word means.
She is naming the direction of the Rabbit.
She is sure she has reached the earth's centre.
explanation: The narrator says Alice has no idea what either term means; she likes how grand the words sound.
sourceQuote: Alice had no idea what Latitude was, or Longitude either

prompt: What does Alice realize after saying “Antipathies”?
options: She has named the wrong country.
The Rabbit has heard her mistake.
The word sounds like a direction.
It does not sound like the right word.
explanation: After saying “Antipathies,” Alice is glad no one hears because she herself senses the word sounds wrong.
sourceQuote: it didn’t sound at all the right word

prompt: Why does Alice decide not to ask whether she is in New Zealand or Australia?
options: She fears she will seem ignorant and decides not to ask.
She already sees the country's name on a sign.
She thinks the Rabbit will tell her soon.
She cannot speak while she is falling.
explanation: She decides not to ask because she fears seeming ignorant, and instead hopes to find the country's name written somewhere.
sourceQuote: what an ignorant little girl she’ll think me for asking! No, it’ll never do to ask

prompt: What is unusual about Alice's attempt to curtsey?
options: She curtseys to the Rabbit as it runs away.
She tries to curtsey while falling through the air.
She curtseys after landing in the hall.
She pretends to curtsey to her sister.
explanation: The narration points out she tries to curtsey while falling through the air, an awkward action in that situation.
sourceQuote: she tried to curtsey as she spoke—fancy curtseying as you’re falling through the air!

prompt: What does Alice hope someone will remember to do for Dinah?
options: Take Dinah along to the garden.
Keep Dinah away from the Rabbit.
Give Dinah her saucer of milk at tea-time.
Let Dinah sleep beside her sister.
explanation: Alice worries Dinah will miss her and hopes someone remembers the cat's saucer of milk at tea-time.
sourceQuote: I hope they’ll remember her saucer of milk at tea-time

prompt: Why does Alice switch from asking whether cats eat bats to whether bats eat cats?
options: She decides the Rabbit may know the answer.
She thinks bats are more like mice.
She wants to ask Dinah a different question.
She cannot answer either question, so either order seems much the same.
explanation: Alice cannot answer either version of the cats-and-bats question, so she says reversing it makes little difference.
sourceQuote: as she couldn’t answer either question, it didn’t much matter which way she put it

prompt: What does Alice ask Dinah in her dream?
options: Whether Dinah has ever eaten a bat.
Whether Dinah can find the Rabbit.
Whether Dinah wants her saucer of milk.
Whether Dinah has seen the garden.
explanation: In her dream she walks hand in hand with Dinah and asks whether Dinah has ever eaten a bat.
sourceQuote: Now, Dinah, tell me the truth: did you ever eat a bat?

prompt: Where does Alice land when the long fall ends?
options: On a stack of bookshelves.
In the Rabbit's waistcoat pocket.
On a heap of sticks and dry leaves.
In a pool at the bottom of the well.
explanation: The fall ends when Alice lands on sticks and dry leaves; the passage then leads her toward another hall.
sourceQuote: down she came upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall was over

prompt: What happens to the Rabbit when Alice turns the corner behind it?
options: It waits beside a little table.
It is no longer in sight.
It jumps back into the well.
It disappears through the tiny door.
explanation: After Alice turns the corner, the Rabbit has disappeared from view; she is close behind it but cannot see it.
sourceQuote: but the Rabbit was no longer to be seen

prompt: How is the long, low hall lit?
options: By a tiny lamp on the table.
By daylight through windows.
By candles carried by the Rabbit.
By a row of lamps hanging from the roof.
explanation: The hall is long and low, and lamps hanging from its roof provide the light; they are not on the table.
sourceQuote: a long, low hall, which was lit up by a row of lamps hanging from the roof

prompt: What does Alice do after finding all the hall's doors locked?
options: She tries every door, then walks sadly down the middle.
She breaks the nearest lock with the key.
She waits by the entrance for the Rabbit.
She climbs the lamps to look for a way out.
explanation: She tests every door while walking around the hall, then sadly heads down the middle when none helps her leave.
sourceQuote: trying every door, she walked sadly down the middle

prompt: What does Alice find on the glass table?
options: A bottle and a little cake.
A book of rules and a ribbon.
Only a tiny golden key.
A saucer and a silver spoon.
explanation: The table holds only a tiny golden key, which Alice wonders might open one of the hall's doors.
sourceQuote: there was nothing on it except a tiny golden key

prompt: Why does the golden key fail to open the hall's doors?
options: The key has been bent out of shape.
The locks are too large or the key is too small.
The doors open only from the other side.
The key is meant for a curtain, not a door.
explanation: Alice finds the key useless because the locks are too large or the key is too small.
sourceQuote: either the locks were too large, or the key was too small

prompt: What leads Alice to notice the little door?
options: She sees it through the glass table.
The Rabbit points to it from the passage.
She hears a lock turn behind the wall.
On a second round, she notices a low curtain she had missed.
explanation: On her second circuit, Alice notices a low curtain she had missed; the small door is hidden behind it.
sourceQuote: on the second time round, she came upon a low curtain she had not noticed before

prompt: How does Alice discover that the golden key fits the little door?
options: She tries it in the lock and it fits.
The key turns when she touches the curtain.
The Rabbit unlocks it for her.
She finds another key inside the door.
explanation: Alice tries the golden key in the little door's lock, and the narrator says it fits to her delight.
sourceQuote: she tried the little golden key in the lock, and to her great delight it fitted

prompt: If Alice could get her head through the doorway, what would still be in the way?
options: Her feet would not fit beneath the door.
Her hair would catch on the lock.
Her shoulders would still prevent her from fitting.
Her hands would be needed to hold the key.
explanation: Alice realizes getting her head through would not solve everything, because her shoulders would still be too large.
sourceQuote: it would be of very little use without my shoulders

prompt: What does Alice wish she could do to fit through the little doorway?
options: Turn into a rabbit for a moment.
Shut up like a telescope.
Make the doorway wider with the key.
Fold herself into the glass table.
explanation: She imagines being able to telescope herself smaller and says that would let her manage the little doorway.
sourceQuote: Oh, how I wish I could shut up like a telescope!

prompt: How do Alice's recent experiences affect what she thinks is possible?
options: She now trusts that every door will open.
She decides only rabbits can change size.
She thinks the garden must be a dream.
She begins to believe very few things are impossible.
explanation: The narrator links Alice's unusual experiences with her belief that very few things are impossible.
sourceQuote: Alice had begun to think that very few things indeed were really impossible

prompt: What does Alice hope to find when she returns to the table?
options: Another key or a book of rules for becoming telescope-like.
A map showing where the Rabbit went.
A note explaining why the doors are locked.
A saucer of milk for Dinah.
explanation: She returns hoping for another key or a book of rules that might teach her how to telescope herself.
sourceQuote: another key on it, or at any rate a book of rules

prompt: What instruction is printed on the bottle's label?
options: OPEN ME
TASTE ME
DRINK ME
SAVE ME
explanation: The bottle's paper label says “DRINK ME” in large letters; the source gives no different instruction.
sourceQuote: the words “DRINK ME,” beautifully printed on it in large letters

prompt: Why does Alice pause to check the bottle's label for poison?
options: She remembers that poison can make a drink dangerous.
She thinks the label may name the garden.
She expects the Rabbit to taste it first.
She wants to see whether it contains milk.
explanation: Alice remembers the warning about poison and checks the label before drinking, following the safety rules she has learned.
sourceQuote: if you drink much from a bottle marked “poison,” it is almost certain to disagree with you

prompt: Why does Alice decide to taste the bottle's contents?
options: She sees the Rabbit drinking from it.
She expects it to make her taller immediately.
The label promises it will open the little door.
It is not marked poison, and she finds it very nice.
explanation: The bottle is not labelled as poison, and Alice finds its taste pleasant, so she finishes it.
sourceQuote: this bottle was not marked “poison,” so Alice ventured to taste it, and finding it very nice

prompt: Why does Alice's face brighten after she shrinks?
options: She thinks she is now the right size for the little door.
She is glad to be taller than the Rabbit.
She believes the garden has moved closer.
She thinks she can reach the key on the table.
explanation: After shrinking, Alice thinks her new height should let her pass through the little door, which makes her pleased.
sourceQuote: only ten inches high, and her face brightened up at the thought that she was now the right size

prompt: What possibility makes Alice nervous enough to wait after shrinking?
options: She may grow so large that she cannot move.
She may fall back into the well.
She may shrink until she disappears altogether, like a candle.
She may forget the way to the table.
explanation: Alice waits to see whether she will shrink further because she fears disappearing altogether, like a candle going out.
sourceQuote: in my going out altogether, like a candle

prompt: What makes climbing to the key difficult for Alice after she shrinks?
options: The key has fallen through the floor.
The table leg is too slippery to climb.
The glass box is locked.
The Rabbit keeps moving the table.
explanation: Though she can see the key, Alice cannot reach it; her attempt to climb a table leg fails because it is slippery.
sourceQuote: up one of the legs of the table, but it was too slippery

prompt: What does Alice do after tiring herself out trying to reach the key?
options: She asks the Rabbit to help.
She goes back through the little door.
She lies down beside the table.
She sits down and cries.
explanation: After tiring herself out trying to climb, Alice sits down and cries; the passage does not say anyone helps her then.
sourceQuote: the poor little thing sat down and cried

prompt: What does the narrator say about the advice Alice gives herself?
options: She gives herself good advice but seldom follows it.
She only takes advice from her sister.
She always remembers advice when she is upset.
She refuses to speak to herself.
explanation: The narrator says Alice gives herself good advice but very seldom follows it, contrasting with her sharp scolding.
sourceQuote: She generally gave herself very good advice, (though she very seldom followed it)

prompt: Why does Alice think eating the cake could help her enter the garden?
options: It might unlock the door without a key.
It might make her remember the rules.
Grow to reach the key or shrink enough to pass under the door.
It might make her able to fly over the table.
explanation: Alice sees two useful outcomes: growing larger could let her reach the key, while shrinking could let her creep under the door.
sourceQuote: I can reach the key; and if it makes me grow smaller, I can creep under the door

prompt: What happens after Alice eats a little piece of the cake?
options: She grows tall enough to reach the key.
She remains the same size.
She shrinks small enough to pass under the door.
She disappears like a candle flame.
explanation: The cake does not change Alice's size after a little piece; the narrator notes this is ordinary, but it surprises her expectations.
sourceQuote: she remained the same size: to be sure, this generally happens when one eats cake

prompt: Why are Alice's feet almost out of sight?
options: They are hidden behind the glass table.
She has stretched so tall that her feet are far below her.
She is lying on one side to reach the door.
The hall's dark end makes them hard to see.
explanation: Her rapid growth has made her feet so distant from her face that she can barely see them.
sourceQuote: they seemed to be almost out of sight, they were getting so far off

prompt: How does Alice plan to send Christmas boots to her feet?
options: Ask the White Rabbit to carry them.
Leave them beside the garden door.
Wait until she shrinks enough to dress them.
Send them by carrier as presents to her feet.
explanation: She imagines addressing a parcel to her own foot, treating it as a distant recipient that needs boots.
sourceQuote: They must go by the carrier,” she thought; “and how funny

prompt: What happens just before Alice hurries toward the garden door?
options: Her head strikes the hall's roof.
The White Rabbit calls her back.
The little golden key falls to the floor.
The garden door swings shut in front of her.
explanation: Her growth carries her head into the hall's roof, interrupting her rush toward the garden.
sourceQuote: her head struck against the roof of the hall

prompt: Why can Alice look through the garden door with only one eye?
options: The keyhole is too small for both eyes.
She is peeking around the White Rabbit.
She is too large to fit upright, so she lies on one side.
The garden light makes her keep one eye closed.
explanation: Because she is too large to fit upright, she lies sideways and can look through with only one eye.
sourceQuote: lying down on one side, to look through into the garden with one eye

prompt: What does Alice's attempt to stop crying reveal?
options: She is pretending to be upset so someone will help.
Her order to herself does not stop her tears.
She is trying to make the pool deep enough to swim.
She has forgotten why she began to cry.
explanation: Alice orders herself to stop, but the crying continues; the scene shows her self-command failing.
sourceQuote: But she went on all the same, shedding gallons of tears

prompt: Why is the White Rabbit hurrying through the hall?
options: He is trying to find the garden key.
He hopes to escape Alice before she sees him.
He has lost his way back to the Duchess's house.
He fears the Duchess will be angry if he keeps her waiting.
explanation: The Rabbit is rushing to the Duchess and fears her anger if he has kept her waiting.
sourceQuote: won’t she be savage if I’ve kept her waiting!

prompt: What happens when Alice timidly tries to ask the Rabbit for help?
options: He drops his things and runs away.
He tells her to wait by the garden door.
He offers her one of his gloves.
He asks her to find the Duchess.
explanation: Her quiet greeting startles the Rabbit; he drops his things and flees instead of stopping to help.
sourceQuote: The Rabbit started violently, dropped the white kid gloves and the fan, and skurried away

prompt: Why does Alice keep fanning herself while she talks?
options: She is trying to make the pool's water move.
She wants to get the White Rabbit's attention.
The hall is hot, so she uses the Rabbit's fan to cool herself.
She is practicing how to wave goodbye to her feet.
explanation: The heat makes Alice use the fan continuously, even while she talks and thinks aloud.
sourceQuote: as the hall was very hot, she kept fanning herself all the time she went on talking

prompt: What question becomes Alice's 'great puzzle'?
options: How can she get the garden door open?
Who is she, if she has changed?
Why is the hall so warm?
Where has the White Rabbit gone?
explanation: After wondering whether she has changed overnight, Alice identifies her own identity as the central puzzle.
sourceQuote: Who in the world am I? Ah, that’s the great puzzle!

prompt: What difference does Alice use to argue she is not Ada?
options: Ada knows all the lessons Alice has forgotten.
Ada lives in a house with very few toys.
Ada has long ringlets, unlike Alice's hair.
Ada has a pet rabbit and Alice does not.
explanation: She contrasts Ada’s long ringlets with her own hair, using appearance to rule Ada out.
sourceQuote: for her hair goes in such long ringlets, and mine doesn’t go in ringlets at all

prompt: Why does Alice think she cannot be Mabel?
options: Mabel is older and has moved away.
Mabel has long ringlets like Ada.
Mabel is afraid of the White Rabbit.
Alice knows many things, while Mabel knows very little.
explanation: Alice sees herself as knowledgeable and Mabel as knowing very little, so she thinks they cannot be the same.
sourceQuote: I know all sorts of things, and she, oh! she knows such a very little!

prompt: What is Alice trying to discover by testing multiplication and geography?
options: Whether she still knows the things she used to know.
Whether she can remember the White Rabbit's name.
Whether Mabel has learned a new language.
Whether the garden lies beyond the English coast.
explanation: She is checking whether familiar learned facts still come to mind as she questions whether she has changed.
sourceQuote: I’ll try if I know all the things I used to know

prompt: Why does Alice think her recited crocodile poem may be wrong?
options: She cannot remember the animal's name.
The words do not come out as she remembers them.
She has never heard the poem before.
The Mouse interrupts before she can finish it.
explanation: The lesson no longer comes out as she remembers, so Alice suspects she has recited it incorrectly.
sourceQuote: the words did not come the same as they used to do

prompt: What does Alice fear would happen if she really were Mabel?
options: She would have to follow the Rabbit to the Duchess.
She would be sent to live beside the garden.
She would have few toys and many lessons in a poky house.
She would have to teach the Mouse French.
explanation: Alice imagines Mabel’s home as restrictive, with few toys and many lessons, and dreads that possibility.
sourceQuote: have next to no toys to play with, and oh! ever so many lessons to learn

prompt: What condition does Alice set before agreeing to return upstairs as Mabel?
options: She must first speak with the White Rabbit.
Someone must bring her more toys.
She must be allowed to keep the golden key.
She wants to know who she is before deciding whether to return.
explanation: She refuses to return on someone else’s label alone, asking to learn who she is first and decide for herself.
sourceQuote: Who am I then? Tell me that first, and then, if I like being that person

prompt: What need does Alice reveal when she cries about being alone?
options: She wants someone to come close and keep her company.
She wants the Rabbit to give back his gloves.
She wants to be left entirely by herself.
She wants to return to her lessons immediately.
explanation: Her wish for someone to appear and her exhaustion from being alone show that she wants company.
sourceQuote: I am so very tired of being all alone here!

prompt: What does Alice infer when she finds the Rabbit's little glove on her hand?
options: The Rabbit has returned and dressed her.
She is shrinking again, making the glove fit.
The hall has become colder while she talked.
The glove has grown larger with her.
explanation: She sees herself wearing one of the Rabbit’s small gloves and concludes her body must be shrinking.
sourceQuote: I must be growing small again.

prompt: How does Alice estimate her height after she notices the glove?
options: She counts the tiles beneath her feet.
She compares herself with the table.
She measures herself against the hall's roof.
She asks the Mouse to guess.
explanation: She uses the table as a height reference, estimating her size by comparing herself with it.
sourceQuote: went to the table to measure herself by it

prompt: What does Alice identify as the cause of her sudden shrinking?
options: The little golden key
The heat in the hall
Her tears in the pool
The fan she is holding
explanation: Alice works out that the fan, rather than an unexplained change, is making her shrink.
sourceQuote: the cause of this was the fan she was holding

prompt: Why does Alice drop the fan hastily?
options: To stop herself from shrinking away altogether.
To make the White Rabbit notice her.
To keep it from falling into the pool.
To use both hands on the garden key.
explanation: She drops the fan because continuing to hold it would make her shrink away altogether.
sourceQuote: she dropped it hastily, just in time to avoid shrinking away altogether

prompt: What does Alice find when she runs back to the garden door?
options: The Rabbit is waiting beside it.
The door is shut and the key is on the glass table.
The key has been carried into the garden.
The door is open, but the pool blocks her way.
explanation: The door is shut again, and the key is still on the glass table as before.
sourceQuote: the little door was shut again, and the little golden key was lying on the glass table

prompt: What does Alice first assume after her foot slips into the water?
options: She has fallen into the Rabbit's bath.
She has reached the garden pond.
She has somehow fallen into the sea.
She has landed in the Mouse's river.
explanation: Before identifying the pool, she mistakes the salty water for the sea and imagines a way back.
sourceQuote: Her first idea was that she had somehow fallen into the sea

prompt: What does Alice expect to find behind the lodging houses on the English coast?
options: A row of bathing machines
A large garden gate
A railway station
A house belonging to the Duchess
explanation: Alice remembers that, on the English coast, a railway station stands behind the lodging houses.
sourceQuote: then a row of lodging houses, and behind them a railway station

prompt: How does Alice finally recognize what she is swimming in?
options: The water tastes exactly like the sea.
It is the pool of tears she shed while nine feet tall.
The White Rabbit tells her where she fell.
She sees the glass table at the bottom.
explanation: She recognizes the water as the tears she shed when she was enormously tall earlier in the chapter.
sourceQuote: she was in the pool of tears which she had wept when she was nine feet high

prompt: What does Alice regret as she swims in the water?
options: Crying so much
Taking the Rabbit's fan
Trying to speak to the Mouse
Leaving the garden door shut
explanation: She worries that her crying may lead to drowning and wishes she had not cried so much.
sourceQuote: I wish I hadn’t cried so much!

prompt: Why does the other swimmer first seem like a much larger animal?
options: Alice mistakes the White Rabbit's ears for a tail.
The water hides the swimmer's head.
A loud splash makes Alice imagine a sea creature.
Alice is so small that she first guesses walrus or hippopotamus.
explanation: The mouse first seems huge, but Alice remembers her tiny size and realizes it is only a mouse.
sourceQuote: at first she thought it must be a walrus or hippopotamus

prompt: Why does Alice think the mouse might be able to talk?
options: She has heard it speak to the Rabbit.
She thinks every mouse learns to speak English.
Everything seems so unusual down there that talking seems possible.
The mouse is wearing the White Rabbit's clothes.
explanation: Because everything feels unusual at her current size, Alice thinks even a mouse may speak.
sourceQuote: Everything is so out-of-the-way down here, that I should think very likely it can talk

prompt: What does Alice borrow from her brother's Latin Grammar to address the Mouse?
options: A list of words for garden plants
A sequence showing how the word 'mouse' changes by case
A rule for turning English into French
A rhyme about animals in water
explanation: She remembers the Latin declension for “mouse” and uses its final form to address the animal.
sourceQuote: “A mouse—of a mouse—to a mouse—a mouse—O mouse!”

prompt: What does Alice guess when the Mouse does not answer in English?
options: It may not understand English and could be French.
It is too tired to hear her.
It is waiting for her to ask about the garden.
It has forgotten how to speak.
explanation: With no reply, Alice guesses the mouse may not understand English and may be French.
sourceQuote: Perhaps it doesn’t understand English,” thought Alice; “I daresay it’s a French mouse

prompt: How does the Mouse react when Alice speaks her French lesson sentence?
options: It begins speaking French back to her.
It swims calmly toward the shore.
It laughs and splashes Alice.
It leaps from the water and trembles with fright.
explanation: The mouse leaps from the water and trembles, showing immediate fright at the French sentence.
sourceQuote: The Mouse gave a sudden leap out of the water, and seemed to quiver all over with fright

prompt: Why does Alice apologize immediately after speaking French?
options: She remembers that she used the wrong Latin case.
She realizes the sentence mentioned a cat, which the Mouse dislikes.
She thinks the Mouse cannot understand her voice.
She remembers the sentence was meant for the Rabbit.
explanation: Alice realizes that her French question mentioned a cat, which she now knows the mouse dislikes.
sourceQuote: I quite forgot you didn’t like cats.

prompt: What does the Mouse ask Alice to imagine after she apologizes for mentioning cats?
options: It asks Alice to imagine liking cats from its point of view.
It says cats are useful for catching rabbits.
It explains that it has never met a cat.
It tells Alice to speak only about dogs.
explanation: The mouse asks Alice to imagine its viewpoint, challenging her to consider why it might dislike cats.
sourceQuote: Would you like cats if you were me?

prompt: Which details does Alice use to make Dinah sound gentle and affectionate?
options: She chases birds through the garden.
She barks when people approach the fire.
She brings Alice gloves and fans.
She purrs by the fire and washes her paws and face.
explanation: Purring by the fire and washing its paws make Dinah sound gentle and affectionate to Alice.
sourceQuote: she sits purring so nicely by the fire, licking her paws and washing her face

prompt: Which part of Alice's description of Dinah most clearly offends the Mouse again?
options: Dinah sits by the fire.
Dinah has soft fur.

The soldiers’ clubs.
The rose-tree’s branches.

The painted roses grow across every path.
A wall separates the arches from the hedgehogs.

The flamingoes carry the arches away from the course.
The Queen orders the soldiers to change places each turn.

The guests play in pairs and follow fixed rules.

prompt: Why does Alice start to worry about her own safety?

The Queen has already ordered the soldiers to seize her.
She thinks the Rabbit has warned the Queen about her.
She cannot find a safe place to hide her flamingo.

prompt: What does Alice first make out in the air?

A crown.
A hedgehog.
A red rose.

The Cat’s paws.
The rest of the procession.
The Queen’s crown.

The players follow too many rules at once.

Help him find the White Rabbit.
Play the next croquet turn for him.

It stays silent and disappears.

The Queen has given the Cat permission to stay.
The Cat has served the King in the past.

The Queen refuses to tell her the order of play.

prompt: Why can’t Alice use her flamingo when she spots two hedgehogs fighting?

The soldiers have turned it into an arch.

The Queen has carried the Cat out of the garden.
The executioner has already beheaded the Cat.

She thinks the Duchess disliked the soup Alice made.

The Duchess refuses to explain her ideas.
The Duchess has forgotten how to speak.
The Duchess dislikes hearing Alice’s opinions.

Games

She starts to mention tasting one, then stops and says she never did.

prompt: How does Alice respond to the unfamiliar dance?

prompt: What correction does the Mock Turtle make to the Gryphon's first formation?
options: The dancers should form two lines, not one.
The dancers should stand in a circle around Alice.
The lobsters should line up behind the turtles.
The dancers should begin in the water.

sourceQuote: Two lines!” cried the Mock Turtle.

prompt: What must happen before the dancers advance?
options: They must find a porpoise to lead them.
They must clear the jellyfish out of the way.
They must throw the lobsters into the sea.
They must return to land in the same order.
explanation: The Mock Turtle places clearing the jellyfish before the advance, and the Gryphon remarks that this usually takes some time.
sourceQuote: when you’ve cleared all the jelly-fish out of the way—

prompt: After the partners are set, what does the Gryphon say the dancers should do?
options: They should leap over the jellyfish.
They should swim after the lobsters.
They should change lobsters and retire in the same order.
They should begin a new line facing the shore.
explanation: The Gryphon adds that the dancers change lobsters and then retire in the order in which they were arranged.
sourceQuote: —change lobsters, and retire in same order,” continued the Gryphon.

options: Turn a somersault in the sea!
Change lobsters again!
Back to land again!
Swim after them!

sourceQuote: Swim after them!” screamed the Gryphon.

prompt: What final movement completes the first figure?
options: The dancers return to land.
The dancers dive after the lobsters.
The dancers form a new line around Alice.
The dancers finish by singing together.

sourceQuote: Back to land again, and that’s all the first figure

They sit sadly and quietly and look at Alice.
They continue jumping until the song ends.
They argue about whose dance steps were correct.

prompt: How do they plan to perform the first figure without real lobsters?
options: They will ask Alice to play a lobster.
They will replace the lobsters with jellyfish.
They say they can do the figure without lobsters.
They decide to skip the first figure.

sourceQuote: We can do without lobsters, you know.

prompt: How does Alice answer the offer to watch the dance?
options: She says she would rather hear a song.
She asks to wait until the lobsters arrive.
She declines because the steps sound dangerous.
She says she would very much like to see it.
explanation: When the Mock Turtle asks whether she would like to see a little of the dance, Alice answers with strong enthusiasm.
sourceQuote: “Would you like to see a little of it?” said the Mock Turtle. “Very much indeed,” said Alice.

prompt: Why does the Gryphon ask the Mock Turtle to sing?
options: The Gryphon has forgotten the words.
Alice asks to hear a song about the sea.
The Mock Turtle has already started a song.
The dance cannot be performed without singing.

sourceQuote: “Oh, you sing,” said the Gryphon. “I’ve forgotten the words.”

prompt: What goes wrong as the pair dance around Alice?
options: They keep dropping the lobsters.
They step on her toes when they pass too close.
They forget which way the first figure goes.
They knock the jellyfish back into the line.
explanation: As the creatures circle Alice, they sometimes come too close and tread on her toes, even while waving their forepaws to the time.
sourceQuote: every now and then treading on her toes when they passed too close

prompt: Why does the whiting urge the snail to walk faster?

The tide is carrying the dancers toward shore.
A porpoise is close behind and treading on the whiting's tail.
The turtles have already begun the next figure.

sourceQuote: There’s a porpoise close behind us, and he’s treading on my tail.

prompt: In the song, what does the whiting say will happen to them?
options: They will be left alone on the shingle.
They will be carried safely to another shore.
They will be asked to lead the dance.
They will be thrown out to sea with the lobsters.
explanation: The whiting warns that they will be taken up and thrown out to sea together with the lobsters, explaining the snail's fear.
sourceQuote: When they take us up and throw us, with the lobsters, out to sea!

prompt: Why does the snail refuse the invitation to dance?
options: He thinks the journey is too far.
He is afraid the porpoise will catch him.
He does not know how to dance with a lobster.
He wants to wait for another shore to appear.

sourceQuote: But the snail replied “Too far, too far!”

prompt: What reassurance does the whiting's friend offer the snail about crossing?
options: The porpoise will carry them across.
There is another shore on the other side.
The lobsters will swim ahead and mark the route.
The journey ends before they leave the shingle.
explanation: The friend answers the snail's worry by pointing out that another shore lies across the water, rather than promising an easier journey.

prompt: What geographical joke appears in the friend's argument?
options: England is said to be on both sides of the sea.
France is described as farther away than England.
Getting farther from England means getting nearer to France.
The song claims that England and France have changed places.
explanation: The friend turns the crossing into a playful trade-off: the farther they travel from England, the nearer they become to France.

prompt: What does the narrator say Alice feels when the song ends?
options: She is eager to hear the song from the beginning.
She is annoyed that the whiting was mentioned.
She wishes she had joined the dance.
She is glad the performance is finally over.
explanation: The narrator directly says Alice feels very glad that the performance is over at last, even though she later praises the song.
sourceQuote: feeling very glad that it was over at last

prompt: Why does the Mock Turtle ask where 'Dinn' may be?

He believes dinner is a kind of whiting.
He thinks Alice has seen fish in a town under the sea.
He wants to know where Alice learned to cook.
explanation: Alice stops in the middle of ‘dinn—,’ but the Mock Turtle pretends that Dinn is a place where she has seen whiting.
sourceQuote: I don’t know where Dinn may be

prompt: Why does the Mock Turtle reject Alice's idea that crumbs cover whiting?
options: Whiting eat the crumbs before anyone sees them.
Crumbs would wash off in the sea.
The fish live too deep for crumbs to reach them.
The crumbs belong only on the lobsters.
explanation: The Mock Turtle says crumbs could not stay on the fish because seawater would wash them off.
sourceQuote: crumbs would all wash off in the sea.

prompt: What prompts the Mock Turtle to hand the explanation over to the Gryphon?

He realizes Alice already knows the answer.
He yawns and shuts his eyes.
He is interrupted by the call about the trial.
explanation: Just as he begins to explain the whiting's tails, the Mock Turtle yawns, shuts his eyes, and asks the Gryphon to continue.
sourceQuote: here the Mock Turtle yawned and shut his eyes.—“Tell her about the reason and all that,”

prompt: According to the Gryphon, what causes the whiting's tails to get stuck in their mouths?

They are bent into position during the dance.
They are caught while the fish swim after lobsters.
They fall a long way after being thrown out to sea.
explanation: In the Gryphon's silly chain of causes, being thrown into the sea makes the fish fall a long way, and that fall traps their tails.
sourceQuote: So they had to fall a long way. So they got their tails fast in their mouths.

prompt: How does the Gryphon explain that shoes are made shiny under the sea?
options: They are done with a whiting instead of blacking.
They are polished with eel oil and sand.
They are rubbed against smooth shells.
They are washed by the sea until they shine.
explanation: Alice says shoes on land are done with blacking, and the Gryphon claims that under the sea a whiting does the job.
sourceQuote: are done with a whiting. Now you know.

prompt: According to the Gryphon, what are undersea boots and shoes made of?
options: Shells and seaweed
Soles and eels
Scales and coral
Leather and sand
explanation: When Alice asks what the shoes are made of, the Gryphon gives the absurd undersea answer ‘soles and eels.’
sourceQuote: Soles and eels, of course,” the Gryphon replied rather impatiently

prompt: What wordplay underlies the Mock Turtle's question, 'With what porpoise?'

It suggests that a porpoise plans the dance.
'Porpoise' sounds like 'purpose,' meaning a reason for the journey.
It uses 'purpose' to mean a kind of sea crossing.
explanation: The joke works because ‘porpoise’ sounds like ‘purpose’: a fish going on a journey might be asked what its purpose is.
sourceQuote: I should say ‘With what porpoise?’

prompt: What first makes Alice nervous as she begins telling her adventures?
options: The Gryphon asks her to explain the dance.
The Mock Turtle interrupts her with a song.
She cannot remember what happened that morning.
The two creatures sit very close and stare with wide eyes and mouths.
explanation: Alice is nervous at first because the creatures crowd close beside her and open their eyes and mouths very wide.
sourceQuote: the two creatures got so close to her, one on each side, and opened their eyes and mouths

prompt: What part of Alice's story makes the Mock Turtle call it curious?
options: Her account of meeting the White Rabbit that morning
Her changed recitation of 'You are old, Father William' to the Caterpillar
Her explanation of why she stopped eating dinner
Her description of dancing around the sea-shore
explanation: The Mock Turtle reacts after Alice recounts repeating the Father William poem to the Caterpillar and getting different words.
sourceQuote: repeating “You are old, Father William,” to the Caterpillar, and the words all coming different

prompt: Why does Alice think she might as well be at school?

The Gryphon gives her a schoolbook to read.
The Mock Turtle asks her to teach the dance steps.
She wants to return to the school where she learned the poem.
explanation: Alice thinks of school because the creatures order her around and make her repeat lessons, much as a teacher might.
sourceQuote: make one repeat lessons!” thought Alice; “I might as well be at school at once.

prompt: Why do the words of Alice's requested recitation come out queerly?

She is trying to copy the Mock Turtle's singing voice.
Her mind is full of the Lobster Quadrille, so she hardly knows what she says.
She has forgotten the poem completely.
explanation: Alice's attention is still on the Lobster Quadrille, leaving her unsure of the words she is supposed to repeat.
sourceQuote: her head was so full of the Lobster Quadrille, that she hardly knew what she was saying

prompt: What change does Alice make to the requested poem's opening?

She changes the poem into a song about soup.
She turns the sluggard into a snail.
She changes the voice of the sluggard to the voice of a lobster.
explanation: The Gryphon asks for ‘the voice of the sluggard,’ but Alice's distracted version begins with the voice of the Lobster.
sourceQuote: ’Tis the voice of the Lobster; I heard him declare,

prompt: Which detail makes the lobster's complaint in Alice's verse absurd?
options: He complains that he was baked too brown and must sugar his hair.
He says a porpoise is stepping on his tail.
He refuses to dance because the sea is too far away.
He asks the whiting to clean his shoes.
explanation: Alice's verse gives the lobster a human-sounding complaint about over-baking and sugaring his hair, rather than a sensible explanation.
sourceQuote: You have baked me too brown, I must sugar my hair.

prompt: What does the Gryphon mean when it says Alice's verse is different from its childhood version?

The wording differs from the version the Gryphon used to say as a child.
The Gryphon had never heard any version of the poem.
Alice has changed the poem into a dance instruction.
explanation: The Gryphon remembers saying a version in childhood and recognizes Alice's words as different from that familiar version.
sourceQuote: That’s different from what I used to say when I was a child

prompt: How does the Mock Turtle judge Alice's version of the poem?

He asks the Gryphon to sing it again.
He has never heard it before but calls it uncommon nonsense.
He says it sounds like the Lobster Quadrille.
explanation: Unlike the Gryphon, the Mock Turtle says he has never heard the verse, though he still judges it to be uncommon nonsense.

Whether the Mock Turtle will finish the song
Whether anything will ever happen in a natural way again

sourceQuote: wondering if anything would ever happen in a natural way again.

She is eager to explain every line.

To locate the court's exit

The White Rabbit
The March Hare

Ask the Dormouse to repeat it
Write down both versions
Send the Hare away

That the jury asked a question

He points to the Dormouse

They cover its mouth with a handkerchief
They send it to the jury-box

prompt: What newspaper phrase does Alice now understand literally?

The witness was called to the stand

The jury reached a verdict

prompt: Why does Alice think the court will now get on better after the second cheer?

The cook has begun giving evidence
The King has stopped asking questions
The jurors have put away their slates

prompt: What wordplay is in the King's reply to the Hatter calling himself poor?

He says the Hatter speaks too quietly
He uses “poor” to mean bad at speaking
explanation: The King repeats “poor” with a different meaning: instead of lacking money, the Hatter is bad at speaking.
sourceQuote: You’re a very poor speaker,” said the King.

prompt: Why can the officer not carry out the Queen's order against the Hatter?

The Hatter is already out of sight
The court blocks the door
The Hatter hides behind the jury

sourceQuote: but the Hatter was out of sight before the officer could get to the door.

prompt: What clue lets Alice recognize the Duchess's cook before she enters?
options: People near the door begin sneezing together
The Dormouse calls out her name
She is carrying a teacup
The Hatter points her out
explanation: Alice recognizes the Duchess's cook because people near the door start sneezing together, matching the cook's pepper-box.
sourceQuote: by the way the people near the door began sneezing all at once.

prompt: How does the cook respond when the King asks her to give evidence?
options: She asks for the White Rabbit
She refuses
She gives the jury a recipe
She leaves without answering
explanation: When the King asks for her evidence, the cook simply refuses instead of answering or explaining.
sourceQuote: “Give your evidence,” said the King. “Shan’t,” said the cook.

prompt: What does the Rabbit tell the King to do with an unwilling witness?
options: Ask the jury to question her
Let the Queen give the evidence
Cross-examine her himself
Call the next witness immediately
explanation: The Rabbit tells the King to question the unwilling witness himself by cross-examining her.
sourceQuote: Your Majesty must cross-examine this witness.

prompt: When asked what tarts are made of, what does the cook answer?
options: Mostly treacle
Bread-and-butter
Pepper and sugar
Pepper, mostly
explanation: Asked directly, the cook says the tarts are mostly pepper; the sleepy voice's “Treacle” is a separate interruption.
sourceQuote: “Pepper, mostly,” said the cook. “Treacle,” said a sleepy voice behind her.

prompt: How does the Queen react when a sleepy voice interrupts the cook?
options: She asks the cook to repeat her answer
She shrieks at the Dormouse
She tells the King to leave
She calls for the March Hare
explanation: The sleepy voice's comment provokes the Queen to shriek at the Dormouse, starting a burst of commands.
sourceQuote: Collar that Dormouse,” the Queen shrieked out.

prompt: What happens to the cook while the court deals with the Dormouse?
options: She disappears
She is put in the canvas bag
She is sent to the jury-box
She starts sneezing
explanation: The court spends time expelling the Dormouse, and when order returns, the cook has vanished.
sourceQuote: by the time they had settled down again, the cook had disappeared.

prompt: What does the King's aside reveal about questioning the next witness?
options: He wants the jury to take over
He believes the cook should return
He finds cross-examining tiring and asks the Queen to do it
He has forgotten how to question witnesses
explanation: Because the questioning makes his forehead ache, the King asks the Queen to cross-examine the next witness.
sourceQuote: It quite makes my forehead ache!

prompt: Who is announced as the next witness at the chapter's end?
options: The Duchess
The March Hare
The Dormouse
Alice
explanation: The Rabbit announces the name Alice as the next witness, ending the chapter with her being called into the trial.
sourceQuote: the White Rabbit read out, at the top of his shrill little voice, the name “Alice!”

prompt: What accidentally sends the jurymen tumbling from their box?
options: Alice's skirt tips the jury-box as she jumps up.
The White Rabbit knocks the jury-box while rushing in.
The Queen strikes the box with her inkstand.
The jurymen lean out to watch Alice grow.
explanation: Alice jumps up in a hurry, and the edge of her skirt overturns the box, spilling the jurymen onto the crowd.
sourceQuote: she tipped over the jury-box with the edge of her skirt

prompt: Why does Alice hurry to collect the fallen jurymen?
options: She thinks they may die if they are not returned to the box.
She fears the King will accuse her of hiding evidence.
She wants to finish the trial before the Queen returns.
She believes the jurymen are trying to escape.
explanation: The goldfish accident comes to mind, so Alice imagines the jurymen must be collected and put back or they will die.
sourceQuote: they must be collected at once and put back into the jury-box, or they would die

prompt: What must happen before the trial can continue?
options: All jurymen must return to their proper places.
Alice must explain why she disturbed the court.
The King must read the evidence aloud again.
The Rabbit must identify the prisoner.
explanation: The King says proceedings cannot continue until every juryman is back in the place assigned to him.
sourceQuote: until all the jurymen are back in their proper places

prompt: What mistake does Alice notice when replacing the jurymen?
options: She has put the Lizard in head downwards.
She has placed the Rabbit among the jurymen.
She has returned the King to the jury-box.
She has left the Lizard outside the courtroom.
explanation: Looking into the box, Alice sees that she put the Lizard in upside down and promptly corrects its position.
sourceQuote: she had put the Lizard in head downwards

prompt: Why does Alice think the Lizard's position may not matter?
options: She thinks either orientation would be equally useful in the trial.
She assumes the Lizard is too stunned to notice.
She believes the King will not look inside the box.
She thinks the jury-box has no proper direction.
explanation: Alice reasons that the Lizard would be just as useful in the trial head-up or head-down, so she doubts the distinction matters.
sourceQuote: quite as much use in the trial one way up as the other

prompt: What do the jurymen do after their slates and pencils are returned?
options: They write a history of the accident.
They prepare a list of questions for Alice.
They record the King's new rule.
They begin copying the verses.
explanation: Once their writing materials are recovered, the jurymen diligently record the accident that upset them.
sourceQuote: they set to work very diligently to write out a history of the accident

prompt: How does Alice answer the King's question about the business?
options: She says she knows nothing whatever about it.
She says she saw the Knave take the tarts.
She says the Rabbit already explained everything.
She says the jury should decide without her.
explanation: Alice twice answers that she knows nothing, even after the King presses her to confirm that she means nothing whatever.
sourceQuote: “Nothing,” said Alice. “Nothing whatever?” persisted the King. “Nothing whatever,” said Alice.

prompt: What correction does the White Rabbit make to the King's description of Alice's answer?
options: He says the King meant 'unimportant,' not 'important.'
He says Alice meant she had seen nothing at all.
He says the King meant 'unusual,' not 'unimportant.'
He says the answer should not be recorded.
explanation: The Rabbit interrupts to replace the King's claim that Alice's answer is important with the opposite word, unimportant.
sourceQuote: Unimportant, your Majesty means, of course

prompt: What does the King's muttering reveal about his choice of words?
options: He is unsure which word, important or unimportant, sounds best.
He is trying to remember the number of the rule.
He is repeating the Rabbit's account of the accident.
He is deciding which juryman should speak first.
explanation: The King alternates between both words under his breath, apparently testing which one sounds better rather than choosing by meaning.
sourceQuote: as if he were trying which word sounded best

prompt: What is Alice's objection to the rule ordering tall people out of court?
options: She says it is not a regular rule and was just invented.
She says the rule applies only to the jurymen.
She says the King has no authority to read from a book.
She says the Queen has already dismissed the court.
explanation: Alice challenges the rule's legitimacy by pointing out that the King has only just invented it, rather than following an established rule.
sourceQuote: that’s not a regular rule: you invented it just now

prompt: How does Alice challenge the King's claim that the rule is the oldest?
options: She argues that the oldest rule ought to be Number One.
She asks the jury to find an older rule in the book.
She says the rule should be numbered after the trial.
She claims the Queen made the rule before the King.
explanation: If the rule really were the oldest, Alice reasons, it should be first in the book rather than numbered forty-two.
sourceQuote: Then it ought to be Number One

prompt: What does the King ask the jury to do just before the Rabbit interrupts?
options: Consider their verdict.
Question the Knave again.
Return the verses to the prisoner.
Choose a new foreperson.
explanation: The King tells the jury to consider its verdict, but the Rabbit interrupts to announce that another piece of evidence has appeared.
sourceQuote: Consider your verdict,” he said to the jury, in a low, trembling voice

prompt: What does the White Rabbit first think the newly found paper is?
options: A letter written by the prisoner to someone.
A list of the jurymen's names.
A note from the Queen to the King.
A record of the tarts that were taken.
explanation: Before opening it, the Rabbit supposes the paper is a letter written by the prisoner to some unnamed person.
sourceQuote: it seems to be a letter, written by the prisoner to—to somebody

prompt: What does the Rabbit discover after unfolding the paper?
options: It is a set of verses, not a letter.
It is a signed confession by the Knave.
It is a list of court rules.
It is an invitation to the tea party.
explanation: After unfolding the paper, the Rabbit recognizes that it contains verses rather than a letter.
sourceQuote: It isn’t a letter, after all: it’s a set of verses.

prompt: What detail about the verses does the Rabbit call queer?
options: They are not in the prisoner's handwriting.
They contain no words about the tarts.
They are written on the outside of the paper.
They are addressed to the Queen.
explanation: The Rabbit says the handwriting is not the prisoner's, which makes the jury wonder who actually wrote the verses.
sourceQuote: No, they’re not,” said the White Rabbit, “and that’s the queerest thing about it.

prompt: What is the Knave's defense against the verses being used as proof?
options: He denies writing them and notes there is no signature.
He says the paper was never found in the courtroom.
He claims the verses were written by the Queen.
He argues that the Rabbit cannot read them aloud.
explanation: The Knave denies authorship and says the lack of a signature means the court cannot prove that he wrote the verses.
sourceQuote: I didn’t write it, and they can’t prove I did: there’s no name signed at the end

prompt: How does the King use the missing signature against the Knave?
options: He claims the unsigned verses show the Knave meant mischief.
He says an unsigned paper cannot be considered evidence.
He argues that the verses must belong to Alice.
He concludes the writer forgot to finish the poem.
explanation: Instead of treating the missing signature as uncertainty, the King calls it suspicious and says an honest writer would sign.
sourceQuote: You must have meant some mischief, or else you’d have signed your name like an honest man

prompt: Why does Alice reject the verses as proof of guilt?
options: The court does not even know what the verses are about.
The verses were written in the King's handwriting.
The Rabbit has not yet read the last line.
The Knave has already confessed to taking the tarts.
explanation: Alice points out that the court cannot use the verses to prove guilt when nobody understands what they mean.
sourceQuote: you don’t even know what they’re about

prompt: What directions does the King give the Rabbit for reading the verses?
options: Start at the beginning, continue to the end, and then stop.
Read the last line first and explain each word.
Skip the confusing parts and read only the evidence.
Ask the jury where the poem should begin.
explanation: The King's instruction is deliberately obvious: begin at the beginning, read through to the end, and stop there.
sourceQuote: go on till you come to the end: then stop

prompt: What is Alice's view of the verses' meaning?
options: She believes there is no meaning in them.
She thinks they explain how the tarts were returned.
She believes they prove the Knave is innocent.
She thinks the poem is a coded message from the Queen.
explanation: Alice says she does not believe the verses contain even an atom of meaning, unlike the King who keeps inventing interpretations.
sourceQuote: I don’t believe there’s an atom of meaning in it

prompt: After Alice offers a reward for explaining the verses, what do the jurymen do?
options: They record her disbelief, but none explains the paper.
They each offer a different interpretation.
They ask the Knave to explain the handwriting.
They refuse to write anything on their slates.
explanation: The jurymen write down that Alice doubts the verses have meaning, but not one attempts to explain them.
sourceQuote: but none of them attempted to explain the paper

prompt: How does the King react to the suggestion that the verses have no meaning?
options: He treats it as a reason not to search for an explanation.
He orders the Rabbit to discard the paper.
He asks the jury to write a new poem.
He decides the Knave must be released.
explanation: The King says that if the verses have no meaning, the court can save effort by not trying to find one.
sourceQuote: we needn’t try to find any

prompt: Which detail from the verses does the King turn into a question to the Knave?
options: The claim that someone could not swim.
The claim that someone had never seen the Queen.
The claim that the tarts were stolen at night.
The claim that someone was too small to read.
explanation: The King seizes on the line about not being able to swim and asks the Knave directly whether he can swim.
sourceQuote: said I could not swim—” you can’t swim, can you?

prompt: Who does the King think is meant by the verse's phrase 'We know it to be true'?
options: The jury.
The Queen and King.
Alice and her sister.
The Knave and the Rabbit.
explanation: The King decides that the collective 'we' in the verse refers to the jurymen, although the poem never identifies them.
sourceQuote: ‘We know it to be true—’ that’s the jury, of course

prompt: How does the King interpret the verse about giving one and two?
options: He thinks it describes what the Knave did with the tarts.
He thinks it describes the jurymen voting twice.
He thinks it describes the Rabbit sharing a meal.
He thinks it describes Alice trading places with the Queen.
explanation: The King connects the poem's counts to the tarts, claiming the lines describe what the Knave did with them.
sourceQuote: that must be what he did with the tarts, you know

prompt: What part of the King's tarts explanation does Alice challenge?
options: She points out that the verses say they all returned from him to you.
She says the poem never mentions tarts at all.
She argues the Knave gave every tart to the jury.
She claims the tarts were still in the kitchen.
explanation: Alice draws attention to the next line, which says the items returned from him to you and complicates the King's explanation.
sourceQuote: they all returned from him to you

prompt: What wordplay does the King make after the Queen denies ever having fits?
options: He uses 'fit' to mean both a seizure and words that suit someone.
He uses 'fit' to mean both a court rule and a punishment.
He uses 'fits' to mean both anger and fear.
He uses 'fit' to mean both handwriting and evidence.
explanation: The King's pun plays on the Queen's denial of having fits and the idea that the poem's words do not fit, or suit, her.
sourceQuote: Then the words don’t fit you,” said the King, looking round the court with a smile

prompt: What order does the Queen demand for the trial?
options: Sentence first and verdict afterwards.
Verdict first and sentence afterwards.
Evidence first and questions afterwards.
Questions first and evidence afterwards.
explanation: The Queen reverses the usual sequence by insisting that punishment be decided before the jury has given its verdict.
sourceQuote: No, no!” said the Queen. “Sentence first—verdict afterwards.

prompt: How does Alice respond when the Queen tells her to hold her tongue?
options: She refuses to be silent.
She apologizes and stops speaking.
She asks the King to answer for her.
She leaves the courtroom without replying.
explanation: Alice directly contradicts the Queen's command, insisting that she will not hold her tongue.
sourceQuote: “Hold your tongue!” said the Queen, turning purple. “I won’t!” said Alice.

prompt: What happens after the Queen orders Alice's head off?
options: Nobody moves.
The King immediately carries out the sentence.
The jury votes to protect Alice.
The Rabbit leads Alice out of court.
explanation: Although the Queen shouts the threat, nobody acts on it; the court's failure to respond precedes Alice's final challenge.
sourceQuote: Off with her head!” the Queen shouted at the top of her voice. Nobody moved.

prompt: What realization makes Alice dismiss the court's power?
options: She recognizes that the court is only a pack of cards.
She realizes that the jurymen have changed sides.
She learns that the Knave has already been acquitted.
She sees that the Queen has left the courtroom.
explanation: Now at full size and unafraid, Alice calls the court a pack of cards, rejecting the authority that had threatened her.
sourceQuote: You’re nothing but a pack of cards!

prompt: What happens instead of the court delivering a verdict?
options: The cards fly at Alice, and the scene shifts to her awakening.
The King declares the Knave guilty and orders his arrest.
The jury explains the verses and frees the prisoner.
The Queen ends the trial and invites everyone to tea.
explanation: After Alice calls them cards, the pack rises and falls on her; the narration moves to her waking rather than announcing a verdict.
sourceQuote: the whole pack rose up into the air, and came flying down upon her

prompt: Where does Alice find herself as the Wonderland scene ends?
options: On the bank, with her head in her sister's lap.
In the courtroom, beside the overturned jury-box.
At the tea table, surrounded by the jurymen.
In the garden, standing beside the Queen.
explanation: Alice's dream gives way to the bank, where she is lying with her head resting in her sister's lap.
sourceQuote: found herself lying on the bank, with her head in the lap of her sister

prompt: What is Alice's sister doing as Alice wakes?
options: Brushing dead leaves from Alice's face.
Gathering the cards from Alice's clothes.
Calling the jurymen back to the court.
Preparing a place for Alice at the tea table.
explanation: The sister gently brushes away leaves that fell onto Alice's face, anchoring the waking scene in the outdoor setting.
sourceQuote: gently brushing away some dead leaves that had fluttered down from the trees upon her face

prompt: What does Alice tell her sister once she wakes?
options: She recounts the strange adventures she can remember.
She describes how the Knave escaped from court.
She explains how to repair the jury-box.
She asks her sister to find the missing verses.
explanation: Alice tells her sister about the strange adventures of the dream, recounting them as well as she can remember.
sourceQuote: she told her sister, as well as she could remember them, all these strange Adventures of hers

prompt: Why does Alice's sister send her in for tea?
options: It is getting late.
The rain is beginning to fall.
The Queen has ordered everyone indoors.
Alice has forgotten to bring the verses.
explanation: After acknowledging Alice's curious dream, the sister tells her to run in for tea because the day is getting late.
sourceQuote: but now run in to your tea; it’s getting late

prompt: What does Alice's sister do after Alice runs off?
options: She watches the setting sun and thinks about Alice's adventures.
She follows Alice into the house for tea.
She searches the bank for the pack of cards.
She returns to the courtroom to question the King.
explanation: The sister remains where she is, watching the sunset and reflecting on Alice and the adventures she has just heard.
sourceQuote: watching the setting sun, and thinking of little Alice and all her wonderful Adventures

prompt: What image of Alice first appears in her sister's dream?
options: Alice's clasped hands and eager eyes looking up at her.
Alice running away with a basket of tarts.
Alice reading verses to the jurymen.
Alice standing beside the shepherd boy.
explanation: The sister imagines Alice's familiar childhood posture, with her hands on her knee and bright eyes turned upward.
sourceQuote: the tiny hands were clasped upon her knee, and the bright eager eyes were looking up into hers

prompt: What familiar sound does the sister imagine replacing the Queen's cries?
options: The voice of the shepherd boy.
The tinkling of sheep-bells.
The lowing of cattle in the distance.
The rustling of grass in the wind.
explanation: In the sister's imagined return to ordinary life, the Queen's shrill commands become the shepherd boy's voice.
sourceQuote: the Queen’s shrill cries to the voice of the shepherd boy

prompt: What does the sister imagine grown-up Alice passing on to other children?
options: Strange stories, perhaps including the old Wonderland dream.
A set of rules for running a courtroom.
A warning never to speak to strangers.
A record of the Knave's trial.
explanation: The sister imagines Alice gathering children and delighting them with strange tales, perhaps retelling the Wonderland dream.
sourceQuote: with many a strange tale, perhaps even with the dream of Wonderland of long ago

prompt: What quality does the sister hope Alice will show toward the children she may gather?
options: She will share their sorrows and take pleasure in their joys.
She will teach them to avoid all imaginative stories.
She will expect them to solve their problems alone.
She will remember only the frightening parts of childhood.
explanation: The sister imagines adult Alice retaining her loving childhood heart by sympathizing with children's sadness and sharing their happiness.
sourceQuote: she would feel with all their simple sorrows, and find a pleasure in all their simple joys
